root_cause.text: The DLL (Delay-Locked Loop) enable state check in the tegra124-emc driver was inverted, causing the code to incorrectly identify when DLL transitions occur because it tested for bit A0 being set (high) when DLL is actually enabled when bit A0 is low.
root_cause.evidence: The patch changes `else if (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)` to `else if (!(timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1))` in the dll_change logic. The CVE description explicitly states "DLL is enabled if bit A0 is low," meaning the condition should check for the bit being clear (0), not set (1). The original code was checking if the bit was set, which is the opposite of the correct logic, causing DLL_CHANGE_ON to be assigned when DLL should be turning off and vice versa.

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix inverted DLL change logic by negating the condition to correctly identify when DLL should be turned on during EMC timing changes.
intent_record.what: Added a logical NOT operator (!) to the condition `timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1` on line 611, changing `else if (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)` to `else if (!(timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1))`.
intent_record.how: This inverts the boolean logic of the condition. Previously, when the least significant bit of timing->emc_mode_1 was 1 (true), dll_change would be set to DLL_CHANGE_ON. Now, when that bit is 0 (false), dll_change is set to DLL_CHANGE_ON. This corrects the DLL (Delay-Locked Loop) state transition logic to properly handle the case when the mode bit transitions from 1 to 0.

grouping_result.intent: Fix inverted DLL change logic by negating the condition to correctly identify when DLL should be turned on during EMC timing changes.

relevance_review.reason: The group directly addresses the inverted DLL enable state check vulnerability by negating the condition to correctly identify when DLL is enabled (bit A0 low). This fix aligns precisely with the root cause of incorrect DLL transition detection in the tegra124-emc driver.

candidates.rationale: This condition checks if bit 0 (A0) is set to determine DLL state, but the root cause indicates the logic is inverted. The condition should be negated because DLL is enabled when bit A0 is LOW (0), not HIGH (1). The equality check causes incorrect identification of DLL transitions.

This condition incorrectly assumes DLL is ON when bit A0 is set (1), but according to the root cause, DLL is actually enabled when bit A0 is LOW (0). The inverted logic causes DLL_CHANGE_ON to be assigned when DLL should actually be turning OFF.

vuln_statements.explanation: This condition checks if bit A0 (0x1) has the same state in both last and timing structures to determine if DLL transition occurs. However, the logic is inverted: DLL is enabled when bit A0 is LOW (0), not HIGH (1). The equality check causes incorrect identification of DLL transitions because it fails to properly detect when DLL state actually changes between enabled (A0=0) and disabled (A0=1) states.

This condition incorrectly assumes DLL is ON when bit A0 is set to 1, but according to the root cause, DLL is actually enabled when bit A0 is LOW (0). This inverted logic causes DLL_CHANGE_ON to be assigned when the DLL should actually be turning OFF, leading to incorrect EMC timing transitions and potential system instability.
